title: Erik Prince Team Pitched White House on El Salvador Detention Camp Plan
description_short: Politico reported that Erik Prince’s team pitched a proposed El Salvador detention and deportation operation; no approval was established.
description_medium: Politico reported on April 11, 2025, that former Blackwater chief Erik Prince and defense contractors pitched the White House on a plan involving a 10,000-person detention camp in El Salvador and transportation for as many as 100,000 people. The article describes a proposal, not an approved contract or an operating program, and says White House interest was unclear.
description_long: On April 11, 2025, POLITICO reported that former Blackwater chief Erik Prince and defense contractors were pitching the White House on a proposal connected to deportations to El Salvador. The proposal described gathering as many as 100,000 people from U.S. prisons, holding them in a 10,000-person detention camp, and flying them to El Salvador. It said Prince’s group, partnering with El Salvador, would handle the logistics and would need access to government immigration files held by law-enforcement agencies to determine people’s immigration status. The proposal claimed a contract would help resolve legal issues and improve the government’s ability to locate, capture, detain, and deport immigrants; those were claims in the pitch, not legal findings. An administration official expected the proposal to be discussed during Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele’s planned White House visit. Prince and the White House declined to comment. POLITICO also reported that an LLC called 2USV was registered in Wyoming, which the article described as an indication that Prince’s group hoped to move to a more serious phase of pitching. The report describes proposed terms and a contractor pitch; it does not report an awarded contract or say the camp or flights began.

supported_facts: POLITICO reports that Erik Prince and defense contractors were pitching the White House on an operation connected to deportations to El Salvador.
The proposal described gathering ‘100,000 of the worst criminal offenders’ from U.S. prisons, holding them at a 10,000-person detention camp, and flying them to El Salvador.

The proposal said Prince’s group would work in partnership with El Salvador, handle logistics, and need access to government immigration files held by law-enforcement agencies to determine immigration status.

The proposal claimed a contract would help resolve legal issues and improve the government’s ability to locate, capture, detain, and deport immigrants; POLITICO attributes this claim to the proposal rather than a legal finding.
An administration official expected the pitch to be discussed during Nayib Bukele’s planned White House visit; Prince and the White House declined to comment.
POLITICO reports an LLC called 2USV was registered in Wyoming and characterizes it as an indication that the group hoped to move to a more serious phase of pitching.
limitations: The article reports proposed terms and a contractor pitch. It does not report an awarded contract or that the camp or flights began.
The proposal’s legal claims are not legal findings; the article does not establish a $100 million agreement, implementation, completed deportations, or a violation of law.

supported_facts: CNN’s April 9 report says the administration had fielded a pitch from Erik Prince for a U.S.-run immigrant detention facility in El Salvador.
CNN reports mixed views among officials about that detention-facility idea, with some seeing potential utility and others viewing it as legally tenuous and unrealistic.
limitations: This is separate earlier reporting and does not establish the April 11 POLITICO proposal’s 10,000-person camp, 100,000-person scale, or specific logistics.
